opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this in terms of a few conditions that all have to hold at once, and the uncomfortable part is that we don't yet know how to check most of them.

The first is that the AI systems have to be *capable enough* to do real safety research: interpretability work, designing evaluations, finding flaws in training setups, red-teaming other models. That's arguably the easiest condition, because capability is what everyone is pushing on anyway. If you get systems that can automate a large fraction of ML research, they can in principle automate a large fraction of alignment research too.

The second, and much harder, condition is that they have to be *trustworthy enough* that you can actually use their output. Either the systems are genuinely trying to help, or you've set things up so that even if some of them aren't, they can't successfully sabotage you. That's where the distinction between alignment and control comes in. Alignment means the model shares your goals. Control means you've built enough oversight, monitoring, and checking that a misaligned model couldn't get away with much. I think realistically we'll need some mix of both, with control carrying more weight early on because we're not confident in our alignment techniques.

The third condition is *verifiability*. A lot of safety research is fuzzy. In capabilities research you get a clear signal: did the benchmark go up, did the loss go down? In alignment research, "Is this interpretability finding real?" or "Does this technique actually make the model honest, or just better at seeming honest?" are much harder to grade. If you can't evaluate the work, you can't train models to do it well, and you can't tell when they're quietly doing it badly. So a big part of the project is converting safety questions into forms where we get crisper feedback.

The fourth is about *time and willingness to spend it*. Even if all the technical pieces are in place, it only works if the developers actually redirect a meaningful fraction of their AI labor toward safety during that critical window, rather than pouring all of it into making the next model more capable. There's a real risk that the window when AIs are smart enough to help but not yet dangerous is short, and competitive pressure pushes everyone to blow right through it. So some of the necessary conditions are institutional: commitments, coordination, maybe regulation that gives labs room to slow down when they need to.

If I had to compress it: the systems need to be capable, sufficiently trustworthy or controllable, working on problems where we can check their output, and deployed by people who are willing to spend that leverage on safety rather than speed. Any one of those failing could sink the whole plan, which is why I think it's a promising strategy but not one we should feel complacent about.

r001.rationale: It describes a critical window when AIs are smart enough to help with safety research but not yet dangerous, and says that window may be short.

r002.rationale: It discusses checking whether safety research outputs are valid, but does not say researchers must recognize when they are approaching that window.

r003.rationale: It gives no minimum duration for the window, such as six months to a year.

r004.rationale: It does not identify AI R&D capability outpacing AI safety research capability as a possible failure of the plan.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big picture is that we're probably going to end up in a world where a lot of the work of aligning and securing AI systems is being done by AI systems themselves, just because the pace at which capabilities are improving is going to outstrip the pace at which humans can do that research on their own. So the question is really, under what conditions does that actually work, rather than just being a story we tell ourselves.

I think there are a few things that need to be true. The first one is that you need the models you're using to help with safety research to actually be trustworthy enough for that task, or at least you need to be able to verify their outputs well enough that trust doesn't matter as much. And those are kind of two different paths. On one path, you've done enough work on the models that you have real confidence they're not, say, subtly sandbagging on safety research or steering you toward approaches that happen to benefit them. On the other path, you don't have that confidence, but the tasks you're handing off are structured so that a human, or a weaker trusted model, can check the work. Like, if the AI is writing code for an interpretability tool, you can test whether the tool works. If it's proposing a conceptual research agenda, that's a lot harder to check.

The second condition is that the overall environment has to actually be set up to let you do this carefully. This is more of a governance and institutional point than a technical one. If you're in a situation where labs are racing, where there's enormous pressure to deploy the next model as quickly as possible, then even if you have the technical capacity to use AI for safety work, you might not have the time or the slack to do it properly. You'd be using AI to accelerate capabilities and sort of sprinkling in some safety work on the side. So I think you need some combination of coordination, regulation, or just a strong enough internal culture that safety work actually gets the compute and the attention it needs.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the one I think about most, is that you need a model of what success looks like that's legible enough that you can tell whether the AI-assisted work is actually making progress. Right now a lot of alignment research is still fairly pre-paradigmatic. We don't have great metrics for how aligned a system is. And if you hand an AI a vague goal like "make the next model safer," you're sort of in the worst position, because you can't verify the output, and you've also made it easy for a misaligned system to produce something that looks like progress. So part of the work humans need to do now, before we're really leaning on AI for this, is building out the evaluations, the benchmarks, the threat models, so that there's something concrete to point the AI at and something concrete to check its work against.

I guess the thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't a plan you can just fall back on by default. People sometimes talk about it as if it's a free lunch, like, "oh, we'll just use AI to solve alignment." But it only works if you've already done a bunch of the groundwork, and if the broader situation gives you room to be careful. If neither of those is true, then you're basically hoping the models are aligned enough to align themselves, which is kind of circular.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls for measurable safety progress, but does not state that researchers must recognize when they are approaching a window for using capable AI safely.

r003.rationale: No minimum duration for the window is stated.

r004.rationale: The candidate discusses misaligned models and competitive pressure, but does not identify AI R&D capability outpacing AI safety research capability as a defeating capability ordering.

astra-6.text:
I think the central thing is that we need some way of checking whether the work the AI is doing is actually helping. It’s not enough to have a very capable model and ask it, “How do we make the next model safe?” If we can’t distinguish a good answer from an answer that sounds reassuring, then we haven’t really solved the problem—we’ve moved it into trusting that model.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we need to understand every step of everything it does. But we need a process where its claims can be tested, where we can find mistakes, and where we have reason to believe it isn’t systematically steering us toward a misleading conclusion. And that process has to remain effective as the AI starts doing work that’s harder for us to evaluate.

The other piece is that there has to be enough time and institutional willingness to use that help. You could have an AI that identifies a serious safety problem, but if the response is, “Well, we’re deploying next week anyway,” that doesn’t get you very far. So I’d want both a technical story about why we can rely on the AI-assisted research and a decision-making process that actually lets the findings change what we build and deploy.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes evaluating AI-assisted research, but does not identify a time window before AI becomes uncontrollably powerful or creates unacceptable risk.

r002.rationale: It does not state that researchers must recognize when they are approaching such a window.

r003.rationale: It gives no duration for a safe-use window and does not mention six months to a year.

r004.rationale: It does not describe AI becoming highly capable at AI R&D while lagging comparably in AI safety research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key condition is that we need some way to tell whether the help we're getting is actually good. It's not enough to have a very capable model produce a safety argument that sounds convincing. We need to be able to check the argument, test the proposed safeguards, and notice when the model is leaving something important out.

And that creates a potential gap: a model might be capable enough to do useful safety research, but also capable enough to mislead us in ways we wouldn't catch. So ideally, we're using models in a regime where they can substantially accelerate our work, while we still have strong reasons to trust—or independently verify—the particular things we're asking them to do.

I also think you need time and an institutional willingness to act on the results. If AI helps you discover a serious problem, but the competitive pressure is such that you're going to deploy anyway, then having that research assistance hasn't solved the problem.

So I'm hopeful about using AI for safety research. But I wouldn't want the plan to be, ‘We'll build something much smarter than us, and then ask it how to make everything safe.’ The question is how we get useful help along the way without making our whole safety case depend on trusting a system we don't yet understand.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a regime where models can accelerate safety work while their outputs remain verifiable, but does not identify a time window before models become uncontrollably powerful or create unacceptable risk.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes checking model outputs, but does not say researchers must recognize when they are approaching a safe-use window.

r003.rationale: The response gives no duration for such a window.

r004.rationale: It describes models that could help with safety research while also misleading researchers, but does not identify the specific ordering of high AI R&D capability without comparable AI safety research capability.
